_note: How a screen introduces itself, in the two tones the founder's prototype gives every phone frame: a lead line saying what the reader is here to do, and an accent line saying what the screen gives them for it. StudioHeadline draws it on iOS and Android and nothing else in either app sets a display-size sentence.
_whyThisIsAContract: Because it was two copies, and both of them said so. WorkspaceNavigation.framing in apps/ios/MyThuso/Features/WorkspaceView.swift and workspaceFraming in apps/android/.../ui/CareStudio.kt each carried the same four pairs with a comment admitting the honest home was a file like this one and that the moment had not come. A headline is the first thing anybody reads on a screen and the cheapest thing in the product to change at eleven at night; two files holding it is how a nurse and a doctor end up being addressed in two slightly different voices by one product.
_whyTheAccentLineIsShort: It is set at the display step, forty points, beside a lead line of the same size. A sentence that runs to three lines there is a paragraph in disguise and the screen has no subject left. The build holds it to 34 characters, which is the longest of the ones the founder actually wrote.
languageNote: The clinical framings are English on every locale, and deliberately. They frame a workspace, and a workspace is the clinical half of this product: packages/catalog/locales.json holds no clinical string and says why — a confidently wrong sentence in a language the reader trusts is worse than an honest English one. The patient's framing is the opposite case and is handled the opposite way: it is the first sentence on the first screen a patient sees, it is not clinical, and it is already in eleven languages, so this contract points at the locale keys rather than restating the words.

framings.why: The prototype's patient frame is "Hello, Nomsa." over "Your next visit. Your team. Your health." What ships is the same shape with the locale contract's own words in it — the greeting and the three-word tagline, both reviewed to the same standard as the rest of the shell and both present in every locale offered. Typing the prototype's second line here would have put a slogan nobody had translated on the one screen every patient opens first, in ten languages, to gain nothing the tagline was not already saying.

framings.surface: The nurse's workspace, on the section it lands on
framings.why: The prototype's nurse frame is "Make today matter." This is the same sentence with the round in it, because a nurse opens this screen at the start of a shift with a list of houses to reach, and "today" alone does not say which today. It was written for the Care Studio pass and has been on both phones since; it is recorded here rather than rewritten, because a headline that changes every time somebody reads the prototype again is a product with no voice.

framings.surface: The doctor's workspace, on the review queue
framings.why: The founder's own, word for word, and the one framing in this file nobody may improve. It says what the product is for on a clinical screen: decision support may draft, and the judgement is the doctor's. The same distinction the standing AI disclosure makes at the foot of every workspace section, made once at the top in the doctor's own terms.

framings.surface: The partner's workspace, on the orders board
framings.why: A pharmacy or a laboratory opens this to find what is stuck, not what is fine. The accent line names the half of the board that is actually the job.

An operator's screen is the only one in this product that is about everybody at once, and the claim it makes is completeness. If the board is ever not every visit, this line is the first thing that has to change.

framings.surface: Live well, the patient's own record of what they did
framings.why: The accent line is the refusal, said as an invitation. packages/catalog/wellbeing.json forbids a score, a grade, a target, a streak, a rank, a percentage and a unit anywhere in that feature, and "in your own words" is what is left when all of those are gone — which is the whole feature rather than a consolation for it.

_whyTheOpeningLinesMovedHere: The same sentences were in apps/web/src/lib/roles.ts as `opensTo` and in apps/ios/MyThuso/Features/WorkspaceView.swift as `WorkspaceNavigation.blurb`, and the iOS comment above them said out loud that they were the web's. Four of the six are shown twice inside the web alone — once on the door a person signs in through, once as the heading of the section they land on — which is why the web already read them back through one function. That function's source was a TypeScript file no other platform can read. This is the same idea with a home all three can reach.

opening.line: Book a nurse, follow a visit, and read what was found at home.
opening.why: Three verbs, in the order a patient does them. It is the one opening line in this file that names no clinical object: a person booking a nurse for their mother is not reading a workspace.

opening.line: Today’s visits, in the order you will do them, and the one still waiting for your sign-off.
opening.why: The last clause is the reason the sentence is this long. A nurse opening the app mid-shift is looking for the thing they have not finished, and a schedule that does not point at it is a list.

opening.line: Cases waiting to be read. Decision support may draft; only a registered doctor signs.
opening.why: The refusal is in the opening line rather than in a notice further down, because it is the whole basis on which a doctor is being asked to look at this screen at all.

opening.line: Prescriptions and laboratory orders routed to this partner, and what each is waiting on.
opening.why: ‘Routed to this partner’ rather than ‘your orders’: a pharmacy sees what was sent to it and nothing else, and the sentence says so before the board does.

opening.line: Where every visit is, which nurses are free, and what is running late.
opening.why: Three questions an operator asks in that order. The claim is completeness — every visit — which is also what the control tower's framing accent line promises.

opening.line: Vetting decisions, the catalogue, growth, finance, and what stands between each capability and being real.
opening.why: The last clause is the readiness list, named on the door rather than found later. The back office is the one role whose job includes knowing what this product cannot yet do.

openingNote: One line per role. Where a role lands on a named section, that section's heading shows this same sentence rather than a second description of one screen — which is what `section` is for and why four of the six have one.

sections.blurb: What went wrong, how severe it is, and who is holding it.
sections.why: Three facts in the order an operator needs them. Deliberately not ‘incidents raised today’: a count belongs to the board under the heading, and a heading that counts is a figure nobody can check.

sections.blurb: Sample collections booked against this partner, and the windows they have to be inside.
sections.why: A collection window is the only thing on that board with a deadline attached, so it is the half of the sentence that earns its place.

sections.blurb: Results this partner has produced, and what is holding each one back from release.
sections.why: ‘Holding back from release’ rather than ‘pending’: a result that exists and cannot be sent is a different problem from one that has not been produced, and the partner is the only party who can tell them apart.

sectionsNote: The sections whose blurb belongs to the screen rather than to somebody's job. A section with nothing useful to say is absent from this list and gets no line, rather than a filler one.

rules.oneHeadlinePerScreen: A display-size headline is a claim the size of the screen. The role framings appear on the section a role lands on and nowhere else; every other section keeps a plain heading. Four display headlines across four tabs are four claims of the same size, which is the inverse of what a display size is for.
rules.neverTyped: No screen may type a lead or an accent line. scripts/check-boundaries.mjs fails the build when one of these strings appears in a native source outside the generated carriers, which is what makes the deletion of the two old copies permanent rather than tidy.
